The Anatomy of a Good Span

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body: > **Prerequisite**: Files 01–07. You understand LLM, RAG, and agent evaluation as scoring functions over outputs and trajectories. This file is about *capturing* those trajectories in production so they can be scored, debugged, and monitored. File 09 (monitoring) consumes what we build here.

sections.title: 1. What is Tracing? (and why it matters for AI)
sections.body:
**Tracing** records the full execution path of a single request, from entry point to final response, including every internal call, branch, and side effect.

A **log** records a discrete event: *"retrieved 5 chunks at 14:02:11"*. Logs are flat — they tell you *what happened*, in isolation. A **trace** records *causal structure*: which span caused which, in what order, with what inputs and outputs. Traces answer *why* and *how*.

For traditional software, this distinction matters but is rarely existential. For AI systems, it is. One user request is almost never one LLM call. It is typically:

- 1 input-classification LLM call (guard or router)
- 1 query-rewrite LLM call
- 1 retrieval call (vector + BM25 + reranker)
- 1 main generation LLM call
- 1+ tool calls (search, calculator, code interpreter)
- 1 output-validation LLM call (safety check)

That's six to ten internal operations per request, often across services, often with branching. A user who reports "the bot gave me a weird answer" generates a complaint that, without a trace, is essentially unfalsifiable — you can't reproduce the failure because you don't know *which* LLM call produced the offending text, *what* context it was given, or *which* tool call returned the bad data upstream.

**Real anecdote.** A support agent product started hallucinating shipping dates at 3 AM. The on-call engineer had only CloudWatch logs showing `INFO LLM call completed` repeated 47 times in the failing minute. No trace IDs. No correlation between sessions and LLM calls. No record of which retrieved chunks were in the prompt. After three hours of guessing, the team added tracing and reproduced the bug in twenty minutes: a stale cache key returned chunks from a *different user's* session. The hallucination was a retrieval bug, not a model bug. They couldn't see it because their logs lacked causal structure.

The lesson: **logs tell you the system ran; traces tell you why it ran the way it did.** For AI, that distinction is the difference between debugging at 3 AM and giving up.

sections.title: 2. Core Concepts: Spans, Traces, Context
sections.body:
### 2.1 Span

A **span** is one unit of work — one LLM call, one tool call, one retrieval. It has a start, an end (so a duration), a name, attributes, and a status.

### 2.2 Trace

A **trace** is a tree of spans representing one complete request. The first span — the entry point — is the **root span**; every other span has exactly one parent. The result is a tree, not a list, because AI work is hierarchical: a request triggers a sub-task, which triggers calls, which trigger further calls.

### 2.3 Parent / child relationship

When span B starts *inside* span A, B is a child of A; A waits for B to finish. Children share the parent's **trace ID** but have their own **span ID**. The parent pointer (`parent_span_id`) is what lets you reconstruct the tree at query time.

### 2.4 Span attributes

Every span carries a flat key/value bag called **attributes**: name, start/end time, input, output, token counts, cost, model, status, plus arbitrary custom fields (`user_id`, `session_id`, `experiment_id`).

### 2.5 Context propagation

**Context propagation** carries the trace ID and current parent span ID across process, thread, async, and service boundaries — in practice, injecting a `traceparent` header (W3C Trace Context) into every outbound HTTP/RPC call and reading it back. Without propagation, a request crossing a service boundary becomes two unconnected traces and the causal chain breaks.

### 2.6 Example: a RAG query trace tree

```
[trace_id: t_abc123]
root: rag.request  (user=u_42, query="What is CRAG?")
├── rag.classify_intent            20ms   intent=question
├── rag.rewrite_query              35ms   rewritten="corrective rag definition"
├── rag.retrieve                   90ms   k=5
│   ├── vector_search              40ms   hits=20
│   └── rerank                     45ms   top_k=5
├── rag.generate                  850ms   model=gpt-4o tokens_in=512 tokens_out=120
└── rag.safety_check               60ms   status=pass
```

The root span captures the whole request. Each child is one step. Sub-children (vector_search, rerank) nest under retrieve. Reading this tree, you can answer: *how long did retrieval take?* (90 ms), *which model was used?* (gpt-4o), *did the safety check pass?* (yes). That is the entire point.

sections.title: 3. The Anatomy of a Good Span
sections.body:
A span is only as useful as the attributes it carries. The minimum viable span has a name and duration; the *useful* span has enough context to be debugged and scored without re-running the request.

### Required attributes (every span)

| Attribute | Why it's required |
|---|---|
| `name` | Semantic, unique-per-step identifier ("rag.retrieve", not "llm_call") |
| `start_time`, `end_time` | Duration, ordering, latency analysis |
| `status` | `ok` / `error` / `timeout` — without this, failures are invisible |
| `trace_id`, `span_id`, `parent_span_id` | Tree reconstruction |

### Required for LLM-call spans

| Attribute | Why |
|---|---|
| `model` | Different models behave differently; you must know which produced the output |
| `input` (prompt or messages) | Without it, you cannot reproduce or score faithfulness |
| `output` (completion) | Same reason |
| `input_tokens`, `output_tokens` | Cost, latency correlation, context-window debugging |
| `cost_usd` | Aggregates to bill-per-request and bill-per-feature |

### Required for tool-call spans

| Attribute | Why |
|---|---|
| `tool_name` | Without it, all tool calls look identical |
| `tool_args` | Reproduction, error diagnosis |
| `tool_result` (or error) | The observation the agent received |
| `duration_ms` | Tool latency is often the dominant cost in agent systems |

### Nice-to-have attributes

| Attribute | Use case |
|---|---|
| `user_id`, `session_id` | Per-user analytics, abuse detection |
| `experiment_id`, `variant` | A/B comparison, rollout tracking |
| `temperature`, `top_p`, `system_prompt_version` | Reproducibility |
| `retrieved_doc_ids`, `relevance_scores` | Retrieval-quality analysis |
| `retries`, `fallback_used` | Resilience analysis |
| `revision_hash` (code version) | Correlating regressions to deploys |

### Anti-patterns to avoid

- Generic names: `"LLM call"` is useless. `"generate_final_answer"` is useful.
- Missing `status` on errors: a failed span with `status=ok` will be silently skipped by error queries.
- Logging only `output` and not `input`: you can score the output but not reproduce the failure.
- Omitting `model`: an eval dataset gathered across two model versions becomes useless.

sections.title: 4. Distributed Tracing for AI (OpenTelemetry)
sections.body:
### 4.1 OpenTelemetry

**OpenTelemetry (OTel)** is the CNCF-incubating, vendor-neutral standard for telemetry — traces, metrics, logs. It defines a span data model, a wire format (OTLP), and language SDKs. It is the de facto industry standard for distributed tracing.

### 4.2 Why OTel for AI?

The promise: instrument once, export anywhere. OTel spans can ship to Jaeger, Tempo, Datadog, Honeycomb, Langfuse, Arize Phoenix, or any OTLP backend — and you can switch backends without re-instrumenting. Without OTel, every tracing tool wants its own SDK and you end up with three competing instrumentation libraries in the same codebase.

### 4.3 OpenLLMetry (Traceloop)

**OpenLLMetry** is an open-source project from Traceloop that adds OTel instrumentation for the AI layer: OpenAI, Anthropic, LangChain, LlamaIndex, Pinecone, Chroma, and dozens more. Install `opentelemetry-instrumentation-openai` and the OpenAI client starts emitting spans with semantic conventions for `llm.request.type`, `llm.prompts`, `llm.completions`, `llm.token_count.prompt`, etc.

### 4.4 OpenInference (Arize)

**OpenInference** is Arize's open specification for AI tracing attributes: richer semantic conventions tailored to AI (`llm.model_name`, `llm.input_messages`, `retrieval.documents`, `tool.name`, `tool.parameters`) that map cleanly to what eval pipelines need. OpenInference and OpenLLMetry are complementary — OpenLLMetry produces the spans, OpenInference defines what attributes they should carry.

### 4.5 The full stack

```
   YOUR APP CODE
        │
        ▼
   OTel SDK  ◄── instrumented by OpenLLMetry / OpenInference
        │  (spans in process memory, batched)
        ▼
   OTel Collector  ◄── optional but recommended: receive, process, sample, route
        │
   ┌────┼─────────────┬─────────────────┐
   ▼    ▼             ▼                 ▼
 Jaeger   Tempo    Langfuse        Arize Phoenix
(trace UI) (Grafana) (AI-eval UI)    (AI-eval UI)
```

The Collector centralizes sampling rules, PII redaction, and routing (e.g., "all LLM spans go to Langfuse; all infra spans go to Tempo"). Skipping it works for prototypes but scales poorly.

sections.title: 5. Popular AI Tracing Tools (comparison)
sections.body:
The market is fragmented. Choose based on (a) whether you need self-hosting, (b) how tightly you're coupled to one framework, and (c) whether you need built-in eval or will run eval separately.

| Tool | Type | Strengths | Weaknesses | Pricing |
|------|------|-----------|------------|---------|
| **LangSmith** | LangChain-native | Tightest LangChain/LangGraph integration; eval + datasets built in; great prompt playground | LangChain bias — non-LangChain apps feel second-class; can get pricey at scale | Free tier, then paid tiers |
| **Langfuse** | Open source | Self-hostable; vendor-neutral; OTel-compatible; explicit eval + datasets + prompt management | Less polished UI than LangSmith; smaller community than LangChain ecosystem | OSS (self-host) + cloud tiers |
| **Arize Phoenix** | Open source | Excellent trace visualizations; OpenInference spec; strong eval suite; works with any framework | Heavier local setup; docs can lag behind features | OSS (self-host) + cloud |
| **Helicone** | Proxy-based | Drop-in reverse proxy — zero code changes; request logging by default; cheap to start | Limited custom spans (proxy sees only API calls, not internal structure); less agent-aware | Free tier + paid |
| **Weights & Biases** | ML platform | Strong ML-ops lineage; experiment tracking; integrates with training runs | Less AI-agent focused; tracing feels bolted-on vs purpose-built | Paid, usage-based |
| **Datadog LLM** | Enterprise | Full APM + LLM observability in one pane; mature alerting; SSO/SOC2 | Expensive; enterprise contract; AI features newer than incumbents | Enterprise |
| **Honeycomb** | Observability | Powerful high-cardinality queries; great for asking arbitrary questions over traces | Steep learning curve; less AI-specific UX (no built-in LLM-as-judge) | Paid, usage-based |
| **Jaeger / Tempo** | Generic OTel | Free, OTel-native, battle-tested | No AI-aware UI; you build eval yourself | OSS |

**Rule of thumb**: start with Langfuse or Phoenix (OSS, free, vendor-neutral); graduate to LangSmith if you live in LangChain, or Datadog/Honeycomb if your org already standardizes on them.

sections.title: 6. Tracing Patterns by System Type
sections.body:
Different system shapes need different span shapes. Below are minimal templates for the five most common patterns.

### 6.1 LLM call tracing

The simplest case. One request, one span.

```
root: llm.request
└── llm.completion  model=gpt-4o  tokens_in=120 tokens_out=45  cost=$0.0007
```

### 6.2 RAG tracing

Adds retrieval spans and document-level attributes.

```
root: rag.request  query="..."
├── rag.retrieve  k=5
│   └── vector_search  hits=20  top_k=5  doc_ids=[d1,d2,d3,d4,d5]
├── rag.generate  model=gpt-4o  context=[d1,d2,d3]  tokens_in=512 tokens_out=120
└── rag.cite_check  cited=[d1,d3]  status=pass
```

### 6.3 Agent tracing (single agent)

ReAct-style trajectory with thought / action / observation spans nested under a loop span.

```
root: agent.run  task="..."
├── agent.step  n=1
│   ├── llm.think  thought="Need to search X"
│   ├── tool.search  args={"q":"X"}  result="..."
│   └── llm.observe  observation="Found Y"
├── agent.step  n=2
│   ├── llm.think  thought="Y is enough; answer"
│   └── llm.final_answer  answer="..."
```

### 6.4 Multi-agent tracing

Per-agent subtrees, plus inter-agent message spans so the conversation between agents is itself visible.

```
root: multi_agent.run  task="..."
├── agent.orchestrator  (planner)
│   └── llm.delegate  to=researcher  msg="find sources on X"
├── agent.researcher
│   ├── tool.search  ...
│   └── llm.respond  to=orchestrator  msg="3 sources: ..."
├── agent.orchestrator
│   └── llm.delegate  to=writer  msg="draft answer using sources"
├── agent.writer
│   └── llm.draft  to=orchestrator  msg="..."
└── agent.orchestrator
    └── llm.final_answer  answer="..."
```

### 6.5 MCP (Model Context Protocol) tracing

When an agent uses MCP tool servers, add a discovery span (listing available tools from a server) plus a per-call span.

```
root: agent.run  task="..."
├── mcp.discover  server=filesystem  tools_found=[read,write,list]
├── mcp.discover  server=git  tools_found=[log,diff,blame]
├── mcp.call  server=filesystem  tool=read  args={path:"/x"}  result="..."
└── mcp.call  server=git  tool=log  args={n:10}  result="..."
```

The discovery span matters: if an agent fails because it didn't know a tool existed, the trace will show `tools_found=[...]` was empty or stale.

sections.title: 7. Building a Trace from Scratch (code)
sections.body:
Before reaching for OTel, it helps to see the model in 50 lines. The script below implements a minimal span class, wraps a mock RAG call (retrieve → generate), and prints the resulting trace tree. Save at `/home/z/my-project/scripts/mini_tracer.py`.

```python
"""Mini tracer: tiny pure-Python span/trace model for a mock RAG call."""
import time, uuid

class Span:
    def __init__(self, name, parent=None, **attrs):
        self.name, self.span_id, self.parent = name, uuid.uuid4().hex[:8], parent
        self.attrs, self.children = dict(attrs), []
        self.start = self.end = None
        self.status = "ok"

    def __enter__(self):
        self.start = time.time()
        if self.parent:
            self.parent.children.append(self)
        return self

    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc, _):
        self.end = time.time()
        if exc_type:
            self.status = f"error:{exc_type.__name__}"
        return False

    def duration_ms(self):
        return round((self.end - self.start) * 1000, 2) if self.end else None

    def render(self, indent=0):
        pad = "  " * indent
        print(f"{pad}|- {self.name} [{self.span_id}] {self.duration_ms()}ms {self.status}")
        for k, v in self.attrs.items():
            vs = str(v)[:57] + "..." if len(str(v)) > 60 else str(v)
            print(f"{pad}    .{k} = {vs}")
        for c in self.children:
            c.render(indent + 1)

def retrieve(query):
    time.sleep(0.01)
    return [f"chunk_about_{query[:8]}", "chunk_about_other"]

def generate(query, docs):
    time.sleep(0.02)
    return f"Answer synthesized from {len(docs)} docs."

def rag_answer(query, root):
    with Span("rag.retrieve", parent=root, query=query, k=2) as s:
        docs = retrieve(query); s.attrs["retrieved"] = docs
    with Span("rag.generate", parent=root, model="gpt-4o",
              input_tokens=42, output_tokens=18, cost_usd=0.0009) as s:
        answer = generate(query, docs); s.attrs["answer"] = answer
    return answer

if __name__ == "__main__":
    root = Span("rag.request", user_id="u_123", session_id="s_9",
                experiment_id="exp_v3")
    with root:
        rag_answer("What is corrective RAG?", root)
    root.render()
```

Output:

```
|- rag.request [a640ba3e] 30.22ms ok
    .user_id = u_123
    .session_id = s_9
    .experiment_id = exp_v3
  |- rag.retrieve [309a6a65] 10.09ms ok
      .query = What is corrective RAG?
      .k = 2
      .retrieved = ['chunk_about_What is ', 'chunk_about_other']
  |- rag.generate [3232076d] 20.09ms ok
      .model = gpt-4o
      .input_tokens = 42
      .output_tokens = 18
      .cost_usd = 0.0009
      .answer = Answer synthesized from 2 docs.
```

Every production tracer does essentially this, plus context propagation, sampling, async support, OTLP export, and a UI — the mental model is the same.

sections.title: 8. Using Traces for Debugging
sections.body:
### 8.1 The trace walkthrough

The most valuable debugging technique is the **trace walkthrough**: pick one failing request, open its trace, read it top-to-bottom as narrative. Most failures become obvious within two minutes. The hallucination that "came out of nowhere" almost always has a retrieve span returning an irrelevant doc, a tool call swallowing an error, or a generate span whose `input` is missing the system prompt you thought was there.

### 8.2 Finding slow spans (latency p95)

Aggregate `duration_ms` per span name across thousands of traces, sort by p95. The top span is your bottleneck. Common findings: reranker calls dominating RAG latency, tool calls to a flaky external API, or a second LLM call waiting on a rate-limit retry. Fixing the top span usually moves p95 more than any model swap.

### 8.3 Finding expensive spans (cost concentration)

Sum `cost_usd` per span name across a day's traces. Often 5% of spans account for 60% of cost. Typical culprit: long-context LLM calls where the prompt is padded with low-value retrieved docs. Cutting retrieval `k` from 10 to 4 can halve cost without hurting faithfulness.

### 8.4 Finding failing spans (error clustering)

Filter traces where `status=error`. Group by `error_type` and span name. If 80% of failures are `tool.timeout` on one external API, that's your problem. If failures cluster on a specific `experiment_id`, you've found a regression.

### 8.5 Finding weird spans (anomaly detection on trace shape)

Trace *shape* is itself a signal. Cluster traces by span tree structure. The majority cluster is "normal"; outlier clusters — extra spans, missing spans, deeper nesting, retries — often correspond to failure modes you didn't know existed. A trace with 14 `agent.step` spans when the median is 3 is a sign of a loop.

### 8.6 Example: debugging a hallucination via trace inspection

```
root: rag.request  query="When was our Series A?"  status=ok  (but answer is wrong!)
├── rag.retrieve  k=5
│   └── vector_search  hits=20  top_k=5  doc_ids=[d1,d2,d3,d4,d5]
│       .note: d3,d4,d5 have relevance < 0.2  (low relevance!)
├── rag.generate  model=gpt-4o  input_tokens=412  context=[d1,d2,d3,d4,d5]
│   .output = "Your Series A was in 2019 for $8M."   ← WRONG. Real answer: 2021.
```

Reading the trace: retrieval returned 5 docs, but 3 had near-zero relevance and were still stuffed into the prompt. The model cited one of the low-relevance docs (an old blog draft) and produced the wrong date. Fix: filter retrieved docs by a relevance threshold before passing to generate. Without the trace, you would have blamed the model.

sections.title: 9. Using Traces for Evaluation
sections.body:
### 9.1 Traces as eval input

The standard offline eval flow is: golden dataset → run → score outputs. Traces upgrade this in two ways: you can sample **real production traffic** as your eval set (with the trace as ground truth for *what the system actually did*), and you can score **per span**, not just per final output.

### 9.2 Span-level metrics

| Metric | Span type | What it scores |
|---|---|---|
| Per-LLM-call faithfulness | generate spans | Is the output supported by the input context? |
| Per-tool-call success | tool spans | Did the tool return a valid, useful result? |
| Per-retrieval context precision | retrieve spans | Are retrieved docs relevant to the query? |
| Per-step decision quality | agent.step spans | Did the agent pick the right action? |

Span-level metrics localize failures. If end-to-end faithfulness is 0.82 but per-LLM-call faithfulness shows 0.95 on the planner and 0.62 on the final-answer generator, you know exactly where to fix.

### 9.3 Trajectory-level metrics from traces

For agents, the trace *is* the trajectory. **Trajectory efficiency** (steps vs minimal), **tool-use accuracy** (correct tool + args), and **trajectory faithfulness** (each observation used appropriately) are all computed directly from the span tree.

### 9.4 Trace-based eval = production-grounded offline eval

The killer pattern: every week, sample 500 production traces, run your eval suite over them (LLM-as-judge, faithfulness, etc.), produce a weekly quality score. This is *production-grounded* — your eval set tracks real distribution drift, not a frozen golden set that ages out. LangSmith, Langfuse, and Arize all support "build dataset from traces" as a first-class operation.

steps.narration: Span-level metrics localize failures. If end-to-end faithfulness is 0.82 but per-LLM-call faithfulness shows 0.95 on the planner and 0.62 on the final-answer generator, you know exactly where to fix.

steps.label: 9.3 Trajectory-level metrics from traces
steps.narration: For agents, the trace is the trajectory. Trajectory efficiency (steps vs minimal), tool-use accuracy (correct tool + args), and trajectory faithfulness (each observation used appropriately) are all computed directly from the span tree.

steps.label: 9.4 Trace-based eval = production-grounded offline eval
steps.narration: The killer pattern: every week, sample 500 production traces, run your eval suite over them (LLM-as-judge, faithfulness, etc.), produce a weekly quality score. This is production-grounded — your eval set tracks real distribution drift, not a frozen golden set that ages out.

sections.title: 10. Privacy & Sampling
sections.body:
### 10.1 PII concerns

Traces contain user data: prompts, retrieved docs, tool args, model outputs. Exporting them to a third-party backend can be a compliance violation (GDPR, HIPAA, SOC2). Before any trace leaves your VPC, it must be scrubbed.

### 10.2 Redaction strategies

| Strategy | How it works | Tradeoff |
|---|---|---|
| **Regex-based** | Pattern-match emails, phones, SSNs, API keys | Cheap, fast, brittle — misses non-canonical forms |
| **NER-based** | Run a named-entity-recognition model to detect PII entities | Better recall, adds latency and a model dependency |
| **LLM-based** | Ask an LLM "redact PII from this span" | Highest recall, highest cost and latency |
| **Field allowlist** | Only export explicitly allowlisted attributes; drop `input`/`output` | Lossiest — kills eval utility but safest |

In practice, combine: regex for known patterns + NER for everything else + field allowlist for high-risk spans. Always redact *before* the collector ships out, not after.

### 10.3 Sampling

Tracing 100% of production requests is rarely affordable at scale. **Sampling** decides which traces to keep.

| Strategy | When to use | Tradeoff |
|---|---|---|
| **Head-based** | Decide upfront at request entry (e.g., 1% of all requests) | Cheap, deterministic, but you'll miss rare errors |
| **Tail-based** | Decide *after* the trace completes (e.g., keep all errors + 1% of successes) | Best for catching failures; requires buffering whole traces |
| **Stratified** | Always keep all errors + 1% of success + 100% of a specific `experiment_id` | Best of both; most production teams converge here |

Tail-based and stratified sampling require a Collector that can buffer a complete trace before deciding — OTel Collectors support this natively via the `tail_sampling` processor.

A common production config: keep 100% of `status=error` traces, 100% of traces with `duration_ms > p99`, 100% of `experiment_id != null` traces, and 1% of everything else. This typically cuts storage 90%+ while preserving every trace you'd actually want to debug.

sections.title: 11. Visual: The Trace Tree
sections.body:
A more elaborate trace, showing a 4-step agent task with all span types labeled. This is the kind of tree a production agent produces on a typical user turn.

```
[trace_id: t_7f3a91]  user=u_42  session=s_204  variant=agent_v6
root: agent.run  task="Draft a 1-pager on Q3 launch"  duration=4.2s  cost=$0.034
│
├── llm.route              90ms   model=gpt-4o-mini  route=planner
│
├── agent.step  n=1  type=plan
│   ├── llm.think          420ms  model=gpt-4o  thought="Need launch date + metrics"
│   ├── tool.search        680ms  q="Q3 launch date"  result="2024-09-12"
│   └── tool.search        710ms  q="Q3 metrics dashboard"  result="DAU 1.2M, +18%"
│
├── agent.step  n=2  type=draft
│   ├── llm.think          510ms  thought="Have date + metrics; retrieve competitor comp"
│   ├── tool.search        640ms  q="competitor Q3 launch"  result="(no results)"
│   └── llm.draft         1100ms  model=gpt-4o  tokens_in=850 tokens_out=620  cost=$0.024
│
├── agent.step  n=3  type=review
│   └── llm.critique       480ms  model=gpt-4o  verdict="needs competitor context"
│
├── agent.step  n=4  type=revise
│   └── llm.revise         620ms  tokens_in=1200 tokens_out=580  cost=$0.008
│
└── llm.final_answer       90ms   status=ok  tokens_out=640
```

Read this trace and you can answer in seconds: *How many steps?* (4.) *Which step cost the most?* (step 2 draft, $0.024.) *Why did the agent revise?* (critique said needs competitor context.) *Was there a tool failure?* (yes — competitor search returned no results.) *Latency bottleneck?* (llm.draft at 1.1s.) Every one of these questions is unanswerable from logs alone.

sections.title: 12. Common Pitfalls
sections.body:
1. **Generic span names.** `"LLM call"` instead of `"generate_final_answer"` — you'll end up with 10,000 spans all named `LLM call` and no way to slice them.
2. **Missing token / cost attributes.** Without these you cannot answer "what's driving my OpenAI bill?" Token counts are cheap and unlock cost analysis.
3. **No error status on failed spans.** A span that threw but recorded `status=ok` is silently invisible to every error query. Always set status in the `except` path.
4. **No trace-ID propagation across async boundaries.** If your agent dispatches to a background task or calls another service and forgets to propagate `traceparent`, the trace breaks into two unconnected pieces.
5. **Tracing 100% in production.** At even modest scale (1M requests/day), this explodes storage and creates a PII surface area you don't need. Sample.
6. **Not redacting PII before export.** Traces contain prompts, and prompts contain user data. Shipping raw prompts to a SaaS backend without redaction may breach GDPR/HIPAA/SOC2 — and you usually won't find out until an audit.
7. **Span explosion from loops.** An agent looping 30 times with 5 spans per iteration produces 150 spans per trace. Set a max-iterations guard and collapse repeated identical steps into a single summary span.
8. **Treating traces as logs.** Traces are trees you query, not "structured logs you can grep." Tools that flatten them into log lines lose the parent/child structure that makes them useful.
9. **Mixing trace IDs across retries.** A retried request should be a new trace (or a new root span with a `retry_of` link), not appended to the original. Otherwise one user's "request" becomes a multi-hour chain.
10. **No revision hash on spans.** Without `revision_hash` (git SHA), you cannot correlate a quality regression to a deploy. Always tag spans with the code version that produced them.
